articles.excerpt: Fixing Unicode (“ñ”) and JSON Serialization Bugs in a Multi‑Platform Content Automation Pipeline TL;DR: I discovered that a single “ñ” in a markdown title broke the JSON payload sent to Bluesky, and a…
articles.body: Fixing Unicode (“ñ”) and JSON Serialization Bugs in a Multi‑Platform Content Automation Pipeline TL;DR: I discovered that a single “ñ” in a markdown title broke the JSON payload sent to Bluesky, and a typo in a key name prevented the Substack payload from being generated. By normalizing Unicode to NFC and correcting the malformed key, the pipeline now produces valid JSON for all targets without silent failures. The Problem My daily publishing bot reads a set of markdown files, injects front‑matter into platform‑specific templates, and writes the result as JSON payloads that are later consumed by CI jobs for Medium, Substack, and Bluesky. On 2026‑11‑06 the bot stopped posting to Bluesky and Substack, even though the console showed no errors.

articles.body: Some games you finish. Some games finish you. And some games you play over and over, convinced that this time you'll figure it out—only to end up in the exact same place, wondering if the problem is the game or the player. Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos (1993) was that game for me. The Setup Westwood Studios (yes, the Command & Conquer people) created Lands of Lore as their take on the first-person dungeon crawler genre that Eye of the Beholder had popularized. The game opens with a simple choice: pick one of four champions to serve King Richard. Each champion had different strengths: Ak'shel — The magic user. Powerful spells, fragile constitution. Michael — The fighter. Strong, durable, magically useless. Conrad — The rogue. Balanced stats, jack of all trades.

articles.excerpt: I build apps, websites and automation for small businesses and founders, and I am one of the four options in this comparison, so I wrote it with my own column kept honest. Four ways to get software bu…
articles.body: I build apps, websites and automation for small businesses and founders, and I am one of the four options in this comparison, so I wrote it with my own column kept honest. Four ways to get software built, compared by what they sell you rather than by what they call themselves. The honest version, including the jobs where I am the wrong answer. Short answer: An agency sells a process and people to point at. A freelancer sells their own hours. A no-code builder sells speed inside a tool's limits. An agentic developer sells what a senior engineer always sold, with faster drafting. The price gap is mostly the cost of the people who are not writing code, not a difference in quality. Agents made the typing cheaper.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove. Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles.
